reviews.checker_notes: All scores 4 or more. Definition and other sense are WordNet's licensed text. Weakest point is the wrong answers: pertinent ("Bearing closely on the question at hand, and so worth raising") follows WordUp's frame ("closely connected with the topic, question... so it clearly deserves attention"), and defunct ("Having stopped operating or existing, as a closed company") follows WordUp's ("A business... that is defunct has stopped existing, working"). Both are reworded, but the structure tracks the source; consider rewriting. pertinent also tempts little. The first sense stresses haste; the word's core is a duty done with minimal interest, which only the other sense covers. "passing" is an ambiguous synonym.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 4, definition 3 (Exceedingly harmful is thin and misses the gradual, hidden quality), plain 3, examples 3 (generic, swappable with harmful), wrongAnswers 1 (no look-alikes; one was the antonym), hook 2 (per- does not mean poison), related 3 (subtle belongs to the other sense). Review round 2: reworded the definition, which followed WordUp phrase by phrase.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: all scores 4 or more. The new definition no longer follows WordUp. It opens with "Causing great harm", the same three words that open Britannica's learner definition ("causing great harm or damage often in a way that is not easily seen or noticed"). The rest is different, so this is short shared wording and scores 4. Weakest point: "spreads" is a little off, because pernicious harm builds up or works unseen and does not have to spread. "builds quietly" would be more exact. Wrong answers: precocious shares only the ending.

reviews.checker_notes: All scores 4 or more. Definition is WordNet's licensed text; "wise" is slightly off, since the word is about seeing clearly rather than wisdom. Wrong answers: pugnacious shares only the -acious ending. The specious wrong answer has the same shape as Cambridge's "seeming to be right or true, but really wrong or false" with different words; acceptable.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 5, definition 3 (thin, Spreading or spread throughout), plain 3 (matched Oxford's definition word for word), examples 2 (six, two fragments), wrongAnswers 1 (no look-alikes), hook 1 (did not name the word, nonsense acronym), related 2 (collective is not an antonym; permeant and permeative are obscure). reviews.checker_notes: All scores 4 or more. Definition echoes WordUp's frame ("spread through a place, group, or activity so widely that..." against "Reaching into every corner of a place, group or system, so that..."); the wording differs, but changing "place, group or system" would remove the echo. The invasive wrong answer ("entry into the body through a cut or an inserted instrument") tracks WordUp's "enters the body, either by making a cut or by inserting a tool"; reword. Choosing invasive's medical sense was right, since its spreading sense is close to the target. "permeating" is a participle rather than a plain adjective.

reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: all scores 4 or more. The new examples show sulking after a refusal (dessert withheld, proposal rejected, scene cut), so the blank now points to petulant. The wrong answers penitent and pellucid share only pe- and tempt little. The hook is a sound-alike (pet), not the real root (Latin petulans, impudent).

reviews.checker_notes: All scores 4 or more. Weakest point: the pilot wrong answer tempts almost nobody, since steering a plane is far from any sense a learner would guess. Everything else is strong, and the hook is true history.

reviews.checker_notes: Round 4. wrongAnswers 3: the deciduous option is original (Longman: 'deciduous trees lose their leaves in winter'; Oxford: 'that loses its leaves every year') and accurate enough. But it is the wrong kind of option. assiduous describes people and their effort, and the other three options (sedentary, audacious, assertive) describe people too. An option that opens 'Of trees and shrubs' is ruled out at a glance, which leaves only three real choices (trap: 'Wrong answers of the wrong kind'; I failed acupuncture under acumen for the same reason). reviews.notes: New word. Taught as the adjective, relevant to the matter at hand. The phrase "apropos of" (with regard to) is common too, but WordNet has no preposition, and keeping one part of speech keeps the quiz options in one form; the hook mentions the phrase. Rewrote WordNet's "Of an appropriate or pertinent nature". Removed the antonym malapropos, which is built on the word and gives the answer away. Avoided propitious and opportune-like look-alikes because of the adverb sense "at an opportune time". Round 2: the reviewer found the apoplectic option followed Longman and the apathetic option followed WordUp's frame. Following the trap on rewrites that keep the old frame, swapped both look-alikes instead of rewording: approximate and apocalyptic, both checked against downloaded dictionary pages.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: apathetic and apoplectic are gone. approximate's option is clean against all sources checked. apocalyptic's option shares the frame 'a disaster so [extreme] that ...' with WordUp ('a coming disaster so extreme that it feels as if everything will collapse') and the idea with Cambridge ('total destruction and end of the world'), but the wording differs; 4. prosaic's option is still near Oxford's 'ordinary and not showing any imagination' but different enough. All five options are plain adjective glosses of 62 to 73 characters against a 74-character definition, so none stands out by style.

reviews.notes: New word. Rewrote WordNet's "Someone with the power to settle matters at will", which sounded like a despot, to the authority whose judgment is final (arbiter of taste, final arbiter). Rewrote the other sense (arbitrator). Dropped the multiword synonym supreme authority. Rewrote WordNet's fragment example. Look-alikes are person nouns that share arb-, -rister or the ab-/art- sound.
reviews.checker_notes: related: arbitrator, umpire and referee fit the other sense (someone picked to settle a dispute) better than the first sense (a final authority, as in arbiter of taste); judge and authority fit. wrongAnswers: abettor's option keeps Cambridge's frame ('someone who helps or encourages another person to do something wrong') with synonyms swapped; barrister's follows Longman's 'a lawyer in Britain who can argue cases in the higher law courts' with the parts reworded and reordered. Both are common phrasing, 4. hook: true but only states the Latin word; little to remember it by.

reviews.notes: New word. WordNet's definition is accurate, but Vocabulary.com shows it word for word, so rewrote it to keep reviewers from reading it as copied. Dropped the spelling variants ascendance, ascendence and ascendency from synonyms. All other fields written from scratch. Look-alikes share the -scend- root (transcendence), asc- (ascription) or the -ance sound and a- start (abeyance, attendance); avoided ascent and ascension, which are close in meaning.
reviews.checker_notes: examples: all four are war or power-struggle settings (kingdom, party faction, board, general and king); more variety would help. wrongAnswers: abeyance and attendance share mostly the -ance ending; attendance's 'a head count' is a loose gloss for the number present. No copying found.

reviews.notes: New word. WordNet led with the chemistry sense (weaken the consistency of a substance); moved the general sense, weaken or reduce the effect of something, to the front and kept the chemistry sense, rewritten, as an other sense. Dropped WordNet's second sense "Become weaker", the same meaning used without an object; added the vaccine sense. Dropped rarefy from synonyms (chemistry sense). Avoided extenuate and accentuate as look-alikes: the first is close in meaning, the second an antonym.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the definition and plain cover the transitive use only; the word is also used intransitively (a signal attenuates). No copying found; look-alikes all share at-/act- and are accurate.

reviews.notes: New word. WordNet's "Influence by slyness" was thin; rewrote the first sense to the charm-to-mislead meaning tests use, and rewrote "Attract; cause to be enamored" as the other sense (charm, enchant). Synonyms now fit the first sense: kept hoodwink, dropped juggle, capture, enamour, trance and catch, added deceive, dupe, cajole and lure. All other fields written from scratch. Look-alikes all share be-.
reviews.checker_notes: examples: all four are swindles (con artist, salesman, startup founder, cult leader); the salesman one is close in scene to Cambridge's example ('The salesman beguiled him into buying a car') though not in wording. Vary the situations. related: cajole means coax with flattery rather than deceive; acceptable but the loosest fit.

reviews.notes: New word: wrote plain, 4 examples, wrong answers and hook from scratch; compared every definition, other sense and wrong answer against downloaded Oxford Learner's, Cambridge, Longman, Dictionary.com, Vocabulary.com, AHD and WordUp pages and reworded every match. Kept the noun sense but rewrote WordNet's definition (a first draft tracked WordUp's 'stirring up the fears, anger and prejudices' and was replaced). Examples avoid living politicians (Cleon is ancient). Look-alikes are person or being nouns: pedagogue, demigod, demographer, ideologue. Dropped synonym demagog (a spelling of the word). Weakest point: ideologue is in the same political field, though it means rigid belief, not stirring up crowds.
reviews.checker_notes: All scores 4 or more. Weakest point, related: agitator and firebrand are broader than demagogue (they stir people up but need not seek power by flattering a crowd). Minor: plain's 'playing on what they fear' is close to WordUp's gloss of the verb, but 'play on fears' is a common idiom.

reviews.notes: New word: wrote plain, 4 examples, wrong answers and hook from scratch; compared every definition, other sense and wrong answer against downloaded Oxford Learner's, Cambridge, Longman, Dictionary.com, Vocabulary.com, AHD and WordUp pages and reworded every match. Kept the inhabitant sense, widened to creatures and regulars. Rewrote the naturalized-species other sense; dropped the old-law 'foreigner with some rights' sense so citizen could serve as a wrong answer (citizen first draft followed WordUp and was rewritten). All wrong answers are person nouns. Dropped rare synonyms habitant and indweller; added visitor and outsider as antonyms. Round 2: replaced all wrong answers. Dropped citizen (near denizen's own resident meaning) and the de-only look-alikes deacon, deserter and dentist; now doyen (French, same sound shape), dissident, dandy and dean, all people-nouns, written from new angles after reading their pages.
reviews.checker_notes: All scores 4 or more. Weakest point, wrongAnswers: doyen tempts well (similar sound, and like denizen it is a person defined by belonging somewhere). dissident tempts moderately (it echoes resident). dandy and dean share only the d and n sounds and are everyday words, so a learner who half knows denizen will rule them out quickly. Wording: the dandy option shares 'careful grooming' and the 'image built around clothes and grooming' frame with WordUp. The dean option lists the same things as Cambridge (a college official responsible for teachers and students). Neither copies a whole definition. Length: the correct option (21 words) is the longest, against 15 to 17 for the wrong ones, which is a mild tell.

reviews.notes: New word: wrote plain, 4 examples, wrong answers and hook from scratch; compared every definition, other sense and wrong answer against downloaded Oxford Learner's, Cambridge, Longman, Dictionary.com, Vocabulary.com, AHD and WordUp pages and reworded every match. Teaches 'impartial, with nothing to gain'. Did not use uninterested or any 'bored' meaning as a wrong answer, since modern usage would make it arguably right. Every example shows someone with no stake judging fairly. Plain first draft tracked WordUp ('nothing to gain from ... judge fairly') and the hook matched WordUp's usage note; both rewritten. Antonyms avoid 'interested' (built on the word). Round 2: rewrote the hook so the gloss of dis- no longer sits next to 'with'.
reviews.checker_notes: All scores 4 or more. The hook now reads clearly. Weakest point: the hook calls the 'stake' sense of interest old, but it is still current (a 20 percent interest in a firm). wrongAnswers is unchanged: the disaffected option adds 'sullen about it', which is not part of that word's meaning.

reviews.notes: New word: wrote plain, 4 examples, wrong answers and hook from scratch; compared every definition, other sense and wrong answer against downloaded Oxford Learner's, Cambridge, Longman, Dictionary.com, Vocabulary.com, AHD and WordUp pages and reworded every match. Replaced the stubbornness synonyms (dogged, tenacious) with mood ones.
reviews.checker_notes: All scores 4 or more. Weakest point, wrongAnswers: dulcet, devout and dormant share little beyond the letter d, so they tempt less than dowdy and durable (durable shares the root durus, which is good). Also: definition's 'keeps others at a distance' adds a claim beyond the core meaning; ex2 ('dour expression' making interns nervous) fits stern or stony equally well; sullen leans to sulky rather than grim.

reviews.notes: New word: wrote plain, 4 examples, wrong answers and hook from scratch; compared every definition, other sense and wrong answer against downloaded Oxford Learner's, Cambridge, Longman, Dictionary.com, Vocabulary.com, AHD and WordUp pages and reworded every match. reviews.checker_notes: All scores 4 or more. Weakest point, wrongAnswers: drab, drowsy, droopy and drastic share only the opening dr/dro, with no shared root or sound beyond that. Also: the hook only restates the French meaning, so it gives little to hold on to; 'often delivered with a straight face' in the definition suits remarks but not droll situations or people; comical is broader than droll.

reviews.notes: New word: wrote plain, 4 examples, wrong answers and hook from scratch; compared every definition, other sense and wrong answer against downloaded Oxford Learner's, Cambridge, Longman, Dictionary.com, Vocabulary.com, AHD and WordUp pages and reworded every match. Weakest point, wrongAnswers: the elevate option's 'promote ... to a higher level' is short phrasing that American Heritage ('promote to a higher rank') and Wordsmyth ('raise or promote to a higher level') share. It is also the only option with two halves joined by 'or'. The liquidate option is in my own words, distinct from Dictionary.com. The definition is close in frame to Longman's (explain something hard by giving more detail) but not copied.

reviews.notes: New word: wrote plain, 4 examples, wrong answers and hook from scratch; compared every definition, other sense and wrong answer against downloaded Oxford Learner's, Cambridge, Longman, Dictionary.com, Vocabulary.com, AHD and WordUp pages and reworded every match. reviews.notes: New word: wrote plain, 4 examples, wrong answers and hook from scratch; compared every definition, other sense and wrong answer against downloaded Oxford Learner's, Cambridge, Longman, Dictionary.com, Vocabulary.com, AHD and WordUp pages and reworded every match. Weakest point, definition: 'when others of its kind were lost or destroyed' overstates the meaning; extant only says a thing still exists (usually where loss was possible), not that others of its kind were lost. Examples: ex2 is close in idea to Dictionary.com's example about only three extant copies; ex3 ('oldest extant groups of reptiles') gives a thin clue, since living or known fit as well.

reviews.notes: New word: wrote plain, 4 examples, wrong answers and hook from scratch; compared every definition, other sense and wrong answer against downloaded Oxford Learner's, Cambridge, Longman, Dictionary.com, Vocabulary.com, AHD and WordUp pages and reworded every match. reviews.notes: Before: sense 2 (WordNet led with the musical medley; the learner needs the imitation-of-style meaning), definition 3, plain/examples/wrongAnswers/hook 1, related 3. Moved the style-imitation meaning to first, kept the medley as an other sense in new words. Wrote plain, 4 examples, 5 wrong answers (pastel, pastoral, panache, pastime, patois; all creative works or style words) and an Italian pasticcio hook. Synonyms trimmed to first-sense words (dropped medley), added antonym original. Compared all text with Oxford Learner's, Cambridge, Longman, Dictionary.com, Vocabulary.com, AHD and WordUp pages for the word and each look-alike; reworded the definition after it tracked WordUp's 'of another artist or era, or mixes' frame. Round 2: replaced pastoral (its option followed WordUp clause by clause) with pastorale, a musical piece, described by its rhythm and the shepherds' piping it imitates.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. Weakest point: the new pastorale option keeps the elements of American Heritage's definition in the same order (instrumental piece, gentle or tender, its rhythm, evoking shepherds' music), with every phrase reworded. Those elements are what a pastorale is, so 4 with this note. Its kind (a musical piece) and length match the other options, and it is a fair look-alike, since learners know pastoral. The definition keeps the two-part frame WordUp and Cambridge share, and the hook's 'a mix of ingredients' echoes Vocabulary.com's note on pasticcio (unchanged from round 1).

reviews.notes: Before: sense 3 (the two WordNet other senses repeated the first or meant compassion), definition 4, plain/wrongAnswers/hook 1, examples 1 (one fragment), related 3. reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The new example 3 no longer fits bathos. Weakest points: examples 3 and 4 are both about a dog, and 'quiet' appears in examples 2 and 3, so the set is a little samey. pomposity is still a weak look-alike (only the initial p). reviews.notes: Before: sense 3 (copper-oxide only, near-duplicate furniture sense), definition 3, plain/examples/wrongAnswers/hook 1, related 1 (none). Chose the physical film on old metal or wood as the first sense, merged the furniture sheen into it, and kept the figurative 'outward look' as the one other sense. All examples use the physical sense. Wrong answers retina, satin, platinum and pectin are all substances or layers. Retina option reworded twice after it tracked Oxford and Random House ('at the back of the eyeball', 'inner lining of the'). Hook gives the true Latin root (patina, shallow dish) as an image, not as a claim about how the sense arose.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point is the wrong answers: pectin shares only p and a final -tin, and retina and satin are rhymes rather than true look-alikes. retina follows WordUp's order (film inside the eyeball that turns light into signals for the brain) and satin swaps the words of American Heritage's 'often silk ... woven ... glossy face and dull back', but both frames are shared by several dictionaries and WordNet. The definition is close to Cambridge's frame (thin layer that develops through use and age) without copying it.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 4, definition 4, plain/wrongAnswers/hook 1, examples 1 (one fragment), related 1 (none). Teaches 'read or inspect closely'. Note: in casual use peruse also means to skim or glance over; the app teaches the careful sense, which is the one tests use, so sense is 4 rather than 5. Antonyms left empty on purpose: skim would contradict the casual sense. Wrong answers pursue, pervade, persuade, perturb (all per- verbs); pursue and persuade reworded after they matched Dictionary.com and Vocabulary.com; perturb avoids Oxford's 'make anxious or unsettled'. Hook root (per- plus use) is Oxford's 'perhaps', so the hook says 'probably'.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the pursue option keeps the 'follow ... in an effort to catch them' frame that Oxford and Longman share; common phrasing, so 4. Sense: the careful-reading meaning is right for tests, though many readers now use the word for skimming; nothing in the entry needs to change for that. The hook's per- plus use, first meaning 'use up', matches American Heritage's etymology.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 4, definition 3 (thin: 'uninterested in intellectual pursuits' leaves out the arts), plain/examples/wrongAnswers/hook 1, related 3. Definition written to cover art and ideas without Oxford's 'hostile or indifferent to culture and the arts'. Kept the ancient people as an other sense since it explains the origin. Wrong answers are all person nouns from phil- or ph- (philanthropist, philatelist, philanderer, pharisee). Hook facts: German student slang Philister for townspeople, popularized in English by Matthew Arnold (Culture and Anarchy, 1869). Round 2: swapped philanderer (compressed WordUp) for palatine, a person noun with the same -tine shape, described as a feudal lord with a king's powers. Rewrote philatelist from a collector's angle (postmarks, misprints, an album) instead of the stock 'collects or studies stamps'.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The new philatelist text matches no downloaded page. palatine is rarer than philistine, so few learners will confuse the two words from memory. Its meaning, a historical figure with a king's powers, is still a plausible guess for a word that also names an ancient people, and it matches the person-noun kind and the length of the other options. Its text echoes Vocabulary.com's 'lord of a palatinate who exercised sovereign power over his lands' and Oxford's 'power in a particular area that a king usually has' in idea but not in wording. The other sense still shares 'what is now ... southern ... coast of Israel ... Gaza' with American Heritage's word history (factual). The hook is accurate but is history more than a memory link.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 2 (WordNet led with the fabric), definition 1 for the learner, plain/examples/wrongAnswers/hook 1, related 4. Chose the noun 'fit of irritation from wounded pride', so no verb examples or verb related words. The fabric is kept as an other sense, rewritten after the first draft tracked WordUp. Definition reworded after it matched WordUp's 'sudden feeling of anger ... wounded pride' frame. Wrong answers piquancy, pity, piety, peek (all p-i or p-ee nouns). Dropped peak: my wording followed WordUp's 'point at which something is' frame, and 4 options are enough. Synonyms checked for first-sense fit (umbrage, huff, resentment).
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest points: two of four examples use the same phrase 'in a fit of pique', so the cloze and new-word card lean on one collocation. Sense: the noun is right, but learners meet the verb ('piqued my interest') at least as often, and the entry does not cover it. Wrong answers: piety blends Collins's 'devotion to God' with Cambridge Academic's 'shown by your worship'; peek swaps every word of Oxford's 'quick and secret look at something you should not be looking at'; both stay at 4 with this note. The definition follows the anger-plus-wounded-pride idea every dictionary uses (WordUp: sudden anger and hurt from wounded pride), reworded enough.

reviews.notes: Before: sense 3 (neutral 'of the masses' misses the snobbish 'unrefined' sense tests use), definition 3, plain/wrongAnswers/hook 1, examples 1 (one fragment), related 3 (vulgar and unwashed lean offensive or slangy). New definition covers both class and the 'lacking refinement' judgment. Added the ancient Roman sense as an other sense. Wrong answers plenary, placid, plangent, pliant (all pl- adjectives); plenary first matched WordUp's 'every member ... rather than a small committee', so it now uses plenary's other meaning, complete and unlimited. Rewrote plenary as a sitting of all delegates, avoiding AHD's 'complete, unlimited' and WordUp's 'rather than a small committee'. Plain no longer opens with 'Plain'. Hook no longer uses AHD's 'the common people of ancient Rome'.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. Weakest point: the wrong answers. plenary, pleonastic and plethoric now share 'ple' with plebeian, which is better than the earlier 'pl' only. pleonastic and plethoric are rarer than plebeian, though, so they act as plausible-sounding ple- adjectives rather than a mix-up learners actually make. protean shares only p and the -ean ending. None of the texts matches a downloaded page: pleonastic avoids Oxford's 'more words than necessary', and plenary covers Cambridge's 'all members present' idea in its own words. The options are shorter (57 to 76 characters) than the 92-character definition, but not enough to give the answer away. The new plain line and hook are clean, and the hook's facts about plebs and patricians are right.

The plain line follows Cambridge's frame (give your opinion ... as if you knew everything) with different words; acceptable but close. Etymology (pontifex) is right.

Example 3 now uses the present tense, portends.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The tense in example 3 is fixed. pertain and portion replace pretend and contend and match no downloaded page. Both share sound with portend, have the same part of speech, and are close in length to the definition. Weakest point: pertain's text is stiff and the shortest option. portion as a verb (ration out) is less familiar than the noun, but it is a real sense. The definition uses the sign-of-something-bad frame Oxford and Longman share.

reviews.notes: New word: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook written from scratch. Before: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook were empty (score 1). Kept WordNet's group sense first and rewrote the definition and the plot sense in my own words. Examples are neutral (office managers, nobles, a board, company founders). Hook uses the true story of Charles II's CABAL ministry (around 1670), which popularized the word; it does not claim the acronym as the origin, and avoids the Hebrew etymology so the hook cannot be read as echoing conspiracy tropes. Look-alikes are all groups of people (cabinet, cadre, caucus, claque, cohort). Junto and camarilla are rare; kept junto, dropped camarilla. Note: cabal and coterie (also in this sheet) are near synonyms, so neither should ever be used as the other's wrong answer. Round 2: swapped the cadre option (followed AHD's frame) for cavalcade, written as a ceremonial ride; rewrote example 4 so caucus no longer fits; replaced the CABAL-ministry hook (it taught the acronym myth) with a spelling hook (starts with cab) that names no group. Main session, round 3: the round 2 hook linked cab by spelling only, but the first syllable is never said as cab, so it is replaced with the true route through French cabale (secret, hidden lore). Checked against downloaded Oxford Learner's, Cambridge, Longman, Dictionary.com, Vocabulary.com, AHD, WordUp and YourDictionary pages: no shared run of 4 words.
reviews.checker_notes: hook 4: the etymology is true. Oxford Learner's, American Heritage, Longman, Dictionary.com and Wiktionary all trace cabal through French cabale and Medieval Latin cabala to the Hebrew word for the Kabbalah, a body of mystical teaching. 'A word for hidden knowledge' is a fair simplification: the Hebrew word literally means received tradition, and the secret sense came from the mystical teaching. Longman glosses the Latin form as 'secret knowledge', so the hook's two-word gloss is close to it, but that is a short, common gloss and not a copied definition. The rest of the hook copies nothing I could find in the nine dictionaries I checked, Wiktionary or Vocabulary.com's note. The hook is neutral: it does not repeat the acronym myth or play into conspiracy tropes, and the link from hidden knowledge to hidden plans is clear. Weakest point: it does not name the Kabbalah, so it is a little vague about what the French word referred to. wrongAnswers 4: cavalcade's option describes an event (a ceremonial ride) while the others describe groups of people, and the claque option shares the common phrase 'people hired to applaud' with WordUp, Wordsmyth and American Heritage. related 4: junto is rare, and conspiracy fits the plot sense more than the group.

Weakest: cavernous and cadaverous describe spaces and looks, not attitudes, so a learner who knows cavalier describes how someone treats things can rule them out. Only 4 wrong answers. reviews.notes: New word. WordNet's gloss "Attack as false or wrong" is right but thin; rewrote it so it covers both people's honesty and claims. reviews.checker_notes: No copying found. The definition's 'seems odd or not to belong there' is clumsy, and it covers only the out-of-place-in-a-setting use, not the 'inconsistent with' use. reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The new manager example fixes the old problem: no wrong answer fits any blank now, and all four examples show favor seeking. No copying found. Weakest: plain combines two common dictionary ideas, the deliberate effort (American Heritage, Vocabulary.com) and someone useful to you (Oxford), in different words. The look-alikes share only in- and -ate. Style: all options are plain verb phrases with no pictures, but infuriate (59 characters) and instigate (55) are clearly shorter than the definition (87).

Round 2: definition rewritten with consistent pronouns; plain now covers written and drawn satire and any target, not only celebrities; swapped lavish (followed WordUp and sat next to the antonyms) and lure (shared only l) for laminate (shares lam-) and harpoon (rhymes on the stressed -poon); reworded the hook away from Oxford's origin note. Replaced with impugn (shares the stressed -pugn/-poon sound and is also done to people with words, but means questioning their honesty, not mocking them) and maroon (rhymes on -oon, done to a person). lament lengthened to match the definition. All checked against downloaded pages from 8 dictionaries: no shared run of 4 words. reviews.checker_notes: Round 4. Only the maroon option changed. It now has no example clause and no island. Every definition of maroon needs abandon or strand plus a remote place, so this is short shared phrasing: 4 with a note. 'Sail off without them' is the writer's own. impugn is not too close to lampoon: it is doubting honesty, with no ridicule or satire. lament and languish copy nothing. Weakest point: style and length. All four options are plain verb phrases, but the definition (104 characters) is still the longest by 25 to 40 characters (options 64 to 79). maroon is now the shortest, which slightly widens the gap from round 3.

But the Old French verb meant 'to accuse' (put a charge upon someone), so the picture of laying a guess on top of the facts is a mnemonic, not the history. That is acceptable but worth knowing. Weakest wrong answer: the new sermonize option keeps the frame that Oxford and Longman share (moral advice given to people who do not want it), in new words. That is common phrasing, since it is what the word means, so it scores 4. Synonyms are better now that 'deduce' is gone. The definition's 'a likely idea of the facts' is still slightly stiff.

reviews.notes: New word: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook written from scratch (before: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook 1, related 3). Four wrong answers (paramount, tantalizing, tangential, tangible). Kept antonym unequal; synonyms equivalent, equal. WordUp has 'ranking above every other concern, so that nothing else should be allowed to push it aside'. That is not a copy under the agreed line, but it is the 'rewrite that keeps the old frame' trap; if anyone flags it again, swap the look-alike rather than reword. tangible now opens with 'having real substance', which Collins, AHD and Webster's New World all use; it is a short shared phrase, so it scores 4 with this note. tantalizing is original. Style: the correct option (16 words) is now clearly longer than the wrong ones (8 to 13 words); keep an eye on that. With 'unequal' removed, related is just two synonyms, which is fine. The definition's clause about the thing not being openly called by that name is still an added nuance.

Dropped rare thralldom/thraldom from synonyms; added servitude, captivity and antonyms freedom, liberty, independence.

The definition describes the control someone has rather than the state of being under it, which fits 'in thrall to' a little awkwardly. Wrong answers: thrift reorders Oxford's frame (the habit of saving money and spending it carefully); throe shares 'wrenching pain' with Wordsmyth. reviews.notes: New word: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook written from scratch (before: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook 1, related 3). reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: the entropy option follows AHD's 'a measure of the disorder or randomness in a closed system' with gauge and physical swapped in. Entropy and tropism are technical and easy to rule out for a word about storytelling, though both (and trophy) truly share the Greek trop- root. Other sense is clean and distinct from the first. Hook checked: Greek tropos 'a turn'.

reviews.notes: New word: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook written from scratch (before: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook 1, related 3). Rewrote the definition to cover both uses (an argument that cannot be defended, a situation that cannot go on) and drop the '(of theories etc.)' label; a first draft matched WordUp's 'so weak or ... flaws' frame. Antonyms changed from reasonable to defensible, sound, justifiable (left out tenable, which is built on the word). Round 2: swapped untenanted (next to untenable's own 'cannot be occupied' sense) for tentative.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The new tentative option is original; it shares no frame with Oxford, Longman, Cambridge or WordUp ('not definite or certain because you may want to change it'). It is a fair look-alike: it shares the 'ten-t' spelling, and a half-knower could confuse a weak position with a provisional one. It comes from Latin tentare 'to try', not tenere, but it shares spelling, not a root claim, so that is fine. Weakest point: untamed shares only the un- prefix. Options are a little shorter than the definition but in the same style.

reviews.notes: New word: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook written from scratch (before: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook 1, related 3). WordNet led with 'improper' only; the definition now leads with 'surprising in an unwelcome way' and keeps 'improper' as a second part, per the brief. Dropped the other sense 'Contrary to your interests or welfare.', which the new definition covers. Replaced the fragment example. Hook is a mnemonic on un- + toward, not a claim of etymology. Synonyms trimmed of uncomely, indecorous; antonyms proper, seemly. Round 2: swapped wayward (one of untoward's own older meanings, unruly) for untidy. Rewrote plain so it keeps the unexpected element. Gave examples 1 and 4 concrete clues (turbulence, burst pipe).
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. wayward is gone, so the two-answer problem is fixed. The new untidy option is original (it shares only 'in a mess' with Collins). As a look-alike, untidy is fair, not strong. It shares 'unt-' and an un- sense of 'not as it should be', which can tempt a half-knower who links untoward with things being amiss. But it describes rooms and desks, while untoward describes events and behavior, so the kind of thing gives it away. The other four options also share only the un- prefix with untoward. Plain and examples are now clear (the added details in examples 1 and 4 give the cloze a real clue). The hook is true but its link to the meaning is still loose.

reviews.notes: New word: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook written from scratch (before: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook 1, related 3). A first draft echoed Cambridge ('larger, stronger, or more ...') and one example echoed a Longman example; both replaced. Look-alikes prestige, vestibule, vestment, vertigo.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: wrong answers. vertigo shares only a few letters with vestige, and its 'whirling or tipping' pairs with WordUp's 'spinning or tilting'. prestige adapts WordNet's gloss ('a high standing achieved through success or influence or wealth') with two words changed; WordNet is licensed, so it is acceptable, but it is the closest text in the entry. Related: 'residue' and 'hint' are a little loose. Hook checked: Latin vestigium 'footprint'.

reviews.notes: New word: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook written from scratch (before: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook 1, related 3). That is short of a copy but close; recast it. Wrong answers lean on dictionary frames: velocity on Cambridge ('the speed at which something is travelling in a particular direction'), volatility on Oxford ('changing easily from one mood to another'), violation on Random House ('a breach ... as of a law'). Each is common phrasing, but there are three. In example 4, 'by free volition' is unidiomatic. 'intention' is a loose synonym. Hook checked: Latin volo 'I wish', the root of voluntary too.

reviews.notes: New word: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook written from scratch (before: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook 1, related 3). Leads with 'deliberate and unprovoked', per the brief; dropped the dated sexual sense and its synonyms (easy, light, loose, promiscuous) and antonym chaste. Avoided WordUp's 'done without reason'. Look-alikes wonted, wan, wanting, waning. Hook etymology (Middle English wan- 'lacking' + towen 'trained') is true but less memorable. Round 2: recast the definition so it no longer reorders Random House's 'deliberate and without motive; unprovoked', and rewrote plain away from Longman. Rewrote the wan option away from Wordsmyth.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2. The new definition is no longer Random House's wording, but its pair 'provoked ... justify' is the idea Collins states as 'without motive, provocation, or justification'. That is common to the meaning, so 4. 'Meant to harm' also fits example 4 (wanton disregard, which is reckless rather than aimed at harm) less well than the others. The plain shares 'cruel or destructive' with Collins ('maliciously and unnecessarily cruel or destructive'); a short shared phrase, so 4. The new wan option is original. Options match the definition's style and length. The hook's last step (from badly brought up to acting for no reason) is still weak.

reviews.notes: New word: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook written from scratch (before: plain, examples, wrong answers and hook 1, related 3). Rewrote the definition in my own words. Wealth is a strong look-alike because 'a wealth of' and 'a welter of' look alike; its option is written as riches, so it is not close to the target, and I removed an example where 'a wealth of statistics' fit the blank. Dropped fuddle, mare's nest, smother from synonyms. Round 2: dropped wealth (it fit 'a ___ of' in three examples) and smelter (shared only the ending). Added weld and welcome (both share wel-), and rewrote welt and welfare from new angles away from AHD and Oxford. Main session, round 3: weld and welcome shared only wel- and were concrete things; welcome followed AHD and welfare followed the 'state of doing well' frame. Now welt, welfare (rewritten), shelter (shares -elter) and welterweight (shares the whole word, the confusion a sports reader would make). swelter was tried and dropped: WordNet has it only as a verb. None fits 'a ___ of' in the examples. Checked against downloaded pages: no shared run of 4 words. Main session, round 4 (one wrong answer left, per the skill): welterweight sat next to welter's informal boxing sense and its closing clause followed Longman, so it is swapped for weather (sounds close to welter, the state of things outdoors). shelter reworded so it no longer mirrors subterfuge's refuge option. Both checked against downloaded pages: no shared run of 4 words.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 4. The weather option is acceptable. It sounds close to welter (/ˈwɛðɚ/ against /ˈwɛltɚ/), so a learner who half knows the word could mix them up by ear. It is also of a fitting kind: a state or condition, a mass noun like welter, unlike the dropped weld and welcome. Its wording follows the stock frame for weather: AHD has 'the state of the atmosphere at a given time and place, with respect to ... temperature, moisture, wind', Dictionary.com and Wordsmyth say much the same, and WordUp has 'what the air outside is like at a given place and time'. This text shares 'the state of the', 'a given' and the air-outdoors idea, but its list and its time phrase are its own, so it is common phrasing and scores 4 with this note. Random House also gives welter a sense of waves or wind tossing about. That is not close to weather in general, but it is worth knowing. shelter no longer mirrors subterfuge's refuge option. It shares 'covered place' and 'danger' with WordUp, Wordsmyth and AHD's usage note; that is common phrasing, so 4 with this note. welt is original. welfare's 'doing well' frame is shared with Webster's New World and Century, as noted in round 3; Merriam-Webster still could not be reached. No option fits 'a ___ of' in any example. Options are 11 to 16 words against a 12-word definition, so the weather option is the longest but not out of style. The definition and hook are unchanged at 4.

reviews.notes: New word. Trimmed related words to the teaching sense. All text compared against downloaded Oxford Learner's, Cambridge, Longman, Dictionary.com, Vocabulary.com, AHD and WordUp pages for the word and each look-alike; reworded the definition, which tracked WordUp's 'guidance given by a tutor'. Definition no longer says long-term or expert; it now describes hands-on teaching in which a more skilled person directs and corrects a learner. Round 3 (main session): intuition rewritten from a new angle (a knack, not a feeling one cannot explain). turbulence (a physical event) swapped for patronage (a kind of support from a patron), written after reading its pages.

Weakest point: 'under the patronage of' is a stock phrase, so patronage nearly fits example 1 ('Under the ___ of a retired concert pianist, the shy teenager learned to play Chopin'); 'learned' still points to tutelage. The definition's 'directs and corrects a learner's work' is a little narrower than all tutelage.

reviews.notes: New word. reviews.notes: New word. Compared every definition, plain, other sense and wrong answer against downloaded Oxford Learner's, Cambridge, Longman, Dictionary.com, Vocabulary.com, American Heritage and WordUp pages for the word and each look-alike; reworded anything that shared a run of four or more content words. Main session: Rewrote moratorium: the old text nearly repeated another word's option for the same look-alike, so a learner would have seen the same wrong answer twice (modicum's).
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: the new moratorium ('A halt called on some activity until a set date or a decision') copies no dictionary. mortality's myth clause still reads unlike the other options. related: singular forms beside a plural noun.

The hook's mori-to-mortal link is the same idea as Vocabulary.com's blurb, though worded differently; moralistic is the weakest look-alike.

reviews.checker_notes: Weakest: microscopic, misanthropic and topical now share the stressed -OP- syllable, and microscopic also shares the 'my' sound, so the set tempts much more. philanthropic shares only the ending -thropic and is the weakest. microscopic's 'measured in millionths of a meter' is narrower than the common meaning (too small to see without a microscope). definition is still close to Merriam-Webster in structure, not wording. The content is different and this is the word's standard collocation, so I accept it. definition: 'whether or not it is what lies underneath' is a little vague. plain shares 'on the surface' with WordUp.
